# Results — Study 500 (Polarity-Flip)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **once price
breaks above a prior swing-high resistance, that broken level flips role and holds as support on
the first pullback** — encoded as a mechanical rule. Resistance levels are confirmed swing-high
fractals (k = 10, with a 10-bar confirmation lag); a level becomes "broken" when the close prints
a clear margin above it; a long fires on the **first pullback retest** into a ±1% band around the
broken level, entered at the **next close** (one documented lag), and we measure the forward
5/10/20/60-day return. Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to
reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **598** mechanical broken-resistance retests pooled across the 5 tapes (k = 10, band ±1%, break buffer +0.5%) |
| Timing / costs | confirmed-fractal levels usable only **+10 bars** later; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per retest |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument level study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline (which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes).

## The signal — broken-resistance retest vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch retest-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = retest − random.

| horizon | n | retest | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (retest−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 598 | +32.4 bps | 60% | +3.81 | +3.6 bps | **+28.7 bps** | +30.4 bps | **+2.05** | **0.040** |
| 10-day | 598 | +45.0 bps | 61% | +3.26 | +17.1 bps | +28.0 bps | +43.0 bps | +1.44 | 0.150 |
| 20-day | 598 | +89.7 bps | 62% | +3.68 | +55.5 bps | +34.2 bps | +87.7 bps | +1.23 | 0.221 |
| 60-day | 595 | +272.1 bps | 68% | +6.34 | +206.1 bps | +66.0 bps | +270.1 bps | +1.47 | 0.141 |

Read it carefully. The one-sample *t* against zero is large at every horizon (**+3.68** at 20
days, **+6.34** at 60) — but most of that is **beta**: long-only entries on an upward-drifting
index inherit the drift, and the random baseline soaks up the bulk of it. Against the
**drift-matched random baseline**, the retest is positive at every horizon, but the difference
only clears the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar at the **shortest horizon**: 5-day Welch *t* = **+2.05**
(*p* = 0.040). By 10 days the edge has decayed below significance (*t* = 1.44) and stays there.
So there *is* a small, short-lived bounce at the first retest — but it fades within two weeks.

## Per-ticker (H = 5) — coherent at the short horizon

| ticker | entries | retest 5d | random 5d | Δ (retest−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 121 | +27.7 bps | +12.6 bps | **+15.0 bps** |
| QQQ | 114 | +51.8 bps | +22.8 bps | **+29.0 bps** |
| IWM | 116 | +46.3 bps | −17.1 bps | **+63.4 bps** |
| DIA | 117 | +9.6 bps | +1.2 bps | **+8.5 bps** |
| GLD | 130 | +27.7 bps | −0.8 bps | **+28.5 bps** |

At the 5-day horizon the retest beats random in **all 5 names** — a coherent cross-section, which
is why the pooled Welch *t* clears 2. This is the strongest evidence in the study.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — the edge frays out at longer horizons

| ticker | entries | retest | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (retest−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 121 | +41.9 bps | +0.96 | +39.1 bps | **+2.9 bps** |
| QQQ | 114 | +179.8 bps | +3.19 | +102.3 bps | **+77.5 bps** |
| IWM | 116 | +31.5 bps | +0.50 | +51.0 bps | **−19.6 bps** |
| DIA | 117 | +27.9 bps | +0.57 | +42.2 bps | **−14.2 bps** |
| GLD | 130 | +162.8 bps | +3.31 | +45.8 bps | **+117.0 bps** |

By 20 days the cross-section is **incoherent**: only QQQ and GLD carry the pooled positive delta;
SPY is flat and IWM/DIA are *behind* random. The 5-day coherence does not persist.

## Level-scramble placebo — geometry is suggestive but not decisive

The "does the specific broken level matter?" test: keep the swing-high **positions** and the
price **marginal**, but permute which level-price sits at which pivot, then re-run the same
break-then-retest logic. If the polarity flip is about *these specific levels*, the scramble
should collapse the result.

| test | observed retest 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY scrambled-level (H = 20) | +41.9 bps | 0.122 | 500 |
| SPY scrambled-level (H = 5)  | +27.7 bps | 0.156 | 500 |

About **12–16%** of scrambled-level runs match or beat the real one — below 50% (so the real
level does a bit better than a random level) but **above 0.05**: the geometry is *suggestive*,
not load-bearing at conventional significance. The broken level is doing *something*, but not
enough to call the role-reversal mechanism proven.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real polarity flip

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* role-reversal bounce (knob `edge`), the same
break-then-retest rule behaves exactly as it must — so the borderline real-tape result is a
genuine measurement, not a dead detector.

| planted edge | n | retest | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no flip) | 83 | −11.4 bps | 43% | −0.20 |
| **0.60** (real planted flip) | 101 | +248.0 bps | 77% | **+5.56** |

With no planted flip the control sits at *t* ≈ 0 (no false positive); a real planted bounce lights
up at *t* = +5.56 with a 77% win-rate. The detector is live and well-calibrated.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The broken-resistance retest **does** beat a drift-matched random baseline
  at the **5-day** horizon — Welch *t* = **+2.05** (*p* = 0.040), with a coherent +Δ across **all
  5 names** — so this is *not* a flat "None". But the edge is small (Δ ≈ +29 bps over 5 days),
  **decays within two weeks** (Welch *t* = 1.44/1.23/1.47 at 10/20/60 days), and the longer-horizon
  cross-section is incoherent (QQQ/GLD carry it, SPY/IWM/DIA don't). A genuine but fragile,
  short-lived bounce — Weak, not Real.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** A real 5-day bounce exists, but it is thin (≈ 29 bps Δ), concentrated
  in two of five instruments at longer horizons, and exposed to slippage on a wide ±1% retest
  trigger; costs trim it and it does not survive past ~10 days. Tradable in principle by a very
  short-horizon mean-reversion desk, but with no margin for error — not something to scale.
- **"Does broken resistance hold as support"? — MIXED.** At the **first** retest, over the **next
  few days**, yes — there is a measurable bounce beyond drift (5-day *p* = 0.040). But it is short
  and the level-scramble placebo does not clear 0.05 (*p* = 0.122), so we cannot attribute the
  bounce decisively to *those specific old-resistance levels* rather than to generic short-term
  mean reversion after a pullback. Partial confirmation — real but unproven mechanism.
